name: Chad
region: East (Ouaddaï, Sila) — Sudanese refugee influx, Lake Chad region
summary: Chad is the primary destination for Sudanese refugees fleeing the Darfur genocide. Over 1.2 million Sudanese refugees have arrived — tripling in two years — in a country that itself ranks 189th on the HDI. Refugees receive only 5 liters of water per day versus the 15–20L standard, only 14% of shelter needs are met, and Sudan's refugee response is only 20% funded.
context:
Chad sits at the intersection of multiple humanitarian crises. It hosts one of the world's most rapidly growing refugee populations — Sudanese fleeing the Darfur genocide and civil war — while simultaneously managing its own internal fragility, Boko Haram violence in the Lake Chad Basin, and recurring drought and flooding from climate change.

The pace of Sudanese refugee arrivals has been extraordinary. The population tripled in two years, reaching over 1.2 million registered Sudanese refugees in Chad — in a country of just 18 million people that itself ranks 189th on the Human Development Index. This is one of the most extreme per-capita refugee burdens of any host country in the world.

Conditions in the refugee sites are alarming. Refugees receive on average only 5 liters of water per day — a third of the Sphere humanitarian standard minimum. Only 14% of shelter needs are met. Health services are stretched beyond capacity. Food rations have been cut due to the chronic underfunding of the Sudan refugee response, which stands at only 20% of requirements.

At the same time, Chad's own population faces severe food insecurity. 7 million Chadians require humanitarian assistance, driven by a combination of Boko Haram violence in the Lake Chad region, recurring floods destroying crops, and structural poverty. The country effectively hosts a mega-crisis while managing its own.

Chad's example illustrates a structural failure of the global humanitarian system: the countries least able to absorb refugees are often those hosting the most, while wealthier nations that could absorb more maintain restrictive policies and under-fund the response in countries like Chad.

donate.name: UNHCR — Chad
donate.description: Registering and protecting over 1.2 million Sudanese refugees and millions of Chadian IDPs, while working to improve desperately inadequate conditions in refugee sites.

donate.name: WFP — Chad
donate.description: Delivering food assistance to Sudanese refugees and food-insecure Chadians, despite chronic underfunding that forces repeated ration cuts.

donate.name: IOM — Chad
donate.description: Supporting displaced people, migrants, and refugees in Chad with emergency shelter, water, and humanitarian assistance.

awareness: Share the water statistic: Sudanese refugees in Chad receive 5 liters of water per day — a third of the minimum humanitarian standard — due to chronic underfunding
Highlight that Chad ranks 189th on HDI yet hosts over 1.2 million Sudanese refugees — the global refugee burden falls most heavily on the world's poorest countries
Raise awareness about the connection between Sudan's war and Chad's crisis — every dollar not spent on stopping the genocide in Sudan creates costs in Chad
Amplify Chadian civil society organizations working on both the refugee response and internal displacement challenges
Challenge donor countries to match their refugee reception policies with adequate funding for countries like Chad that do the actual hosting
political: Demand that your government increase funding to the Sudan refugee response in Chad — 20% funded means 80% of needs go unmet
Urge representatives to press for accountability for the genocide in Sudan that is generating the refugee flows Chad cannot absorb
Advocate for burden-sharing mechanisms that provide real support to frontline host countries like Chad, rather than just symbolic pledges
Support climate adaptation funding for Chad — a country facing both climate-driven drought and flooding in a Lake Chad Basin that has already lost 90% of its surface area
Push for sustained development investment in Chad to build the capacity to host refugees without devastating its own population
